sections.h: Elisha's ministry (2 Kings 2–8)
sections.b: Elisha's own work begins when Elijah is taken up. He picks up his master's cloak, parts the Jordan and is greeted by the sons of the prophets as Elijah's heir (2 Kings 2:1–15). His first acts are a healing and a curse: Jericho's spring made wholesome, and the jeering youths of Bethel mauled by bears (2 Kings 2:19–25). He gives the word that saves three kings' armies in Moab (2 Kings 3), then works a chain of household wonders: a widow's oil, a son for the Shunammite and the boy's return to life, a poisoned stew made safe and bread multiplied (2 Kings 4). He heals Naaman the Aramean and passes Naaman's disease to the lying Gehazi (2 Kings 5). He floats an ax head, foils Aram's raids, blinds an army and feeds it, and promises food to a starving Samaria (2 Kings 6–7). His public ministry ends in Damascus, weeping before Hazael, the man the LORD will use to punish Israel (2 Kings 8:7–15). Elisha works more wonders than any other prophet in the Hebrew Bible, and most of them serve ordinary people.

common: Elisha received a double portion of Elijah's spirit and worked twice as many miracles.
uncommon: Some scholars think many stories now told of Elijah were first told of Elisha, or the reverse.

claude.title: Claude's theory: a prophet who ends in tears
claude.body: My own reading: the Elisha cycle is arranged to move from the bears of Bethel (2 Kings 2:24) to the tears before Hazael (2 Kings 8:11–12), so that the prophet who began with a curse ends grieving over the judgment he must announce.

sections.h: Elijah's last days (2 Kings 1–2)
sections.b: Elijah's last confrontation is with Ahab's son Ahaziah, who sends to ask Baal-zebub of Ekron whether he will recover from a fall. The angel of the LORD sends Elijah to meet the messengers and announce the king's death. Fire from the sky consumes two companies of soldiers sent to seize him; the third captain pleads, and Elijah goes down with him to tell the king face to face (2 Kings 1). The messengers know him by his hairy coat and leather belt (2 Kings 1:8), the dress later worn by John the Baptist. On his last journey from Gilgal through Bethel and Jericho he tries three times to leave Elisha behind, parts the Jordan with his rolled cloak, grants Elisha's request for a double share if he sees him taken, and is carried into the sky in a storm wind as a chariot and horses of fire part them (2 Kings 2:1–12). Elijah does not die, which is why later Scripture can expect his return.

common: Elijah went to heaven in a chariot of fire.
uncommon: The text says the storm wind, not the chariot, took Elijah up; the chariot and horses of fire separated the two men.

sections.h: The guilds in Elisha's day (2 Kings 2–6)
sections.b: The sons of the prophets appear most often in the Elisha stories. Groups at Bethel and Jericho know in advance that Elijah will be taken (2 Kings 2:3, 2:5); fifty of them watch from a distance as he crosses the Jordan, greet Elisha as heir, and insist on a three-day search (2 Kings 2:7, 2:15–18). They had wives and debts (2 Kings 4:1), met before Elisha at Gilgal in famine (2 Kings 4:38), shared food brought as firstfruits (2 Kings 4:42–44), and built a larger meeting place by the Jordan with borrowed tools (2 Kings 6:1–7). One of them anoints Jehu (2 Kings 9:1). The picture is of communities, perhaps poor, gathered around a leading prophet whom they called master (2:3, 2:5; 6:5).

common: The sons of the prophets were a school for training prophets.
uncommon: Some scholars think the guilds were the first tellers and collectors of the Elisha stories.

sections.h: Mesha's revolt and the war of 2 Kings 3
sections.b: After Ahab's death Moab broke away from Israel (2 Kings 1:1; 2 Kings 3:5). Its king Mesha, a sheep breeder, had paid a vast tribute of lambs and wool. Jehoram of Israel, with Jehoshaphat of Judah and the king of Edom, marched around the south of the Dead Sea, nearly died of thirst, and was saved by Elisha's word of water. The allies ravaged Moab and besieged Kir-hareseth, but when Mesha offered his firstborn son as a burnt offering on the wall, great wrath came on Israel and they withdrew (2 Kings 3:4–27). Mesha's own inscription, the Mesha Stele found at Dhiban in 1868, tells of Omri's oppression, Mesha's revolt, and his capture of Israelite towns, crediting the god Chemosh. The two accounts agree that Moab won its freedom but tell different parts of the war.
sections.refs: 2 Kings 1:1; 2 Kings 3:4–27; Numbers 21:29; Isaiah 15:1–9; Jeremiah 48:1–47; Amos 2:1–3

common: The Mesha Stele confirms the Bible's account of the war with Moab.
uncommon: The Stele does not mention the southern campaign of 2 Kings 3, and some think it was set up before that war.

sections.h: Aram in the Elisha stories (2 Kings 5–8)
sections.b: In 2 Kings 5–8 Aram of Damascus is Israel's constant enemy. Its raiders carry off an Israelite girl, who sends Naaman, Aram's commander, to Elisha for healing (2 Kings 5:1–19). Its king sets ambushes that Elisha keeps exposing, and sends an army to Dothan to seize him, which is struck blind, led into Samaria, fed and released (2 Kings 6:8–23). Ben-hadad's siege of Samaria brings famine and horror, ended when the Arameans flee at a sound the Lord makes them hear (2 Kings 6:24–7:16). At last Elisha goes to Damascus, where the sick Ben-hadad sends Hazael to ask whether he will live, and Elisha foresees that Hazael will be king and will savage Israel (2 Kings 8:7–15). Assyrian records name the king of Damascus in these years Hadad-ezer and confirm that Hazael, a usurper, followed him.

common: Ben-hadad was the name of only one king of Damascus.
uncommon: Many historians think the Aramean war stories of 2 Kings 6–7 first belonged to the later reigns of Jehu's dynasty.

sections.h: The end of Omri's house begins (2 Kings 1–8)
sections.b: Omri's dynasty continues through Ahab's sons. Ahaziah reigns two years and dies after consulting Baal-zebub (2 Kings 1:2–17). His brother Jehoram removes a Baal stone his father made but keeps Jeroboam's sins (2 Kings 3:1–3), loses Moab, and endures Aram's siege of Samaria (2 Kings 6:24–33). The family's reach grows into Judah through marriage: Jehoram of Judah marries Ahab's daughter, and their son Ahaziah, whose mother Athaliah is called a daughter of Omri, walks in the ways of Ahab's house (2 Kings 8:18, 8:26–27). The Mesha Stele names Omri as Moab's oppressor and says that his son meant to oppress it too. By the end of 2 Kings 8 both kings, Joram of Israel and Ahaziah of Judah, stand together at Jezreel, where Jehu will strike them both.

uncommon: The Mesha Stele's phrase about Omri's son has been read by some as meaning his grandson, to reconcile it with Kings.

sections.h: Samaria under siege (2 Kings 6–7)
sections.b: Samaria is the setting for some of the darkest and brightest scenes of the Elisha stories. Naaman comes to the king there and Elisha sends for him (2 Kings 5:3–8). The blinded Aramean army is led into the city, fed and freed (2 Kings 6:19–23). Then Ben-hadad's siege drives prices to madness: a donkey's head for eighty shekels, dove's dung for five, and two mothers who agree to eat their sons (2 Kings 6:24–30). Elisha promises that the next day flour and barley will sell cheaply in Samaria's gate. Four men with skin disease find the Aramean camp abandoned, the people plunder it, and the doubting officer is trampled in the gate (2 Kings 7:1–20). Excavations at Sebastiye have uncovered the royal acropolis of Omri's and Ahab's city.

uncommon: Some scholars think the siege of 2 Kings 6–7 was a literary expansion of the covenant curses rather than a remembered event.

sections.h: Baal-zebub and the Baal stone (2 Kings 1; 3)
sections.b: The war with Baal continues after Carmel. The injured king Ahaziah sends to ask Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron, whether he will recover, and Elijah asks whether there is no God in Israel (2 Kings 1:2–6). The name Baal-zebub has been read as Lord of Flies, a mocking change of an original Baal-zebul, Prince Baal, a title known from Ugarit. The Greek translators wrote Baal Fly. In the New Testament Beelzebul is a name for the prince of demons (Mark 3:22; Matthew 12:24). Ahab's son Jehoram removes the standing stone of Baal his father had made, though Jehu will later destroy Baal's stone and temple in full (2 Kings 3:2; 2 Kings 10:26–27). In the Elisha stories the LORD gives rain, oil, children, life and bread, all of which Baal's worshipers looked to Baal for.
sections.refs: 2 Kings 1:2–16; 2 Kings 3:2; 2 Kings 4:1–44; 2 Kings 10:26–28; Mark 3:22; Matthew 12:24

common: Beelzebub means Lord of the Flies.
uncommon: Many scholars think the original name was Baal-zebul, Prince Baal, and that zebub, fly, is a scribal insult.

sections.h: Parting the Jordan and the healing waters (2 Kings 2; 5; 6)
sections.b: The Jordan is crossed and recrossed in 2 Kings. Elijah strikes it with his rolled cloak, and he and Elisha cross on dry ground; Elisha strikes it with the same cloak on his return, and the water parts again (2 Kings 2:8, 2:13–14). The crossings retell Joshua's entry into the land and point back to the Red Sea. Naaman, scornful at first of a muddy river compared to Damascus' Abana and Pharpar, dips seven times in the Jordan and is healed (2 Kings 5:10–14). By the Jordan the sons of the prophets cut timber, and Elisha makes a lost ax head float (2 Kings 6:1–7). The fleeing Arameans leave a trail of dropped gear all the way to the Jordan (2 Kings 7:15). Christian readers later linked the river of Naaman's healing with Jesus' baptism.
sections.refs: 2 Kings 2:6–14; 2 Kings 5:10–14; 2 Kings 6:1–7; 2 Kings 7:15; Joshua 3:14–17; Luke 4:27

uncommon: Some interpreters read Elijah's crossing east of the Jordan as a return to the place where Moses died.

sections.h: Elisha heals Jericho's spring (2 Kings 2)
sections.b: Elijah and Elisha pass through Jericho on Elijah's last day, where a group of the sons of the prophets lives (2 Kings 2:4–5). Fifty of them watch the crossing of the Jordan and later search for Elijah (2 Kings 2:7, 2:15–18). The town's leaders tell Elisha that the place is pleasant but the water is bad and the land loses its young. He throws salt from a new bowl into the spring, and says in the LORD's name that it is healed, and it stays healed to the narrator's day (2 Kings 2:19–22). Readers have connected the bad water to Joshua's curse on whoever rebuilt the city (Joshua 6:26; 1 Kings 16:34). The spring at Tell es-Sultan is still called Elisha's Spring.

uncommon: E. V. Hulse suggested that Jericho's bad water carried schistosomiasis, a parasite spread by water snails that causes sickness and miscarriage.

sections.h: The youths of Bethel (2 Kings 2)
sections.b: Bethel, the shrine of Jeroboam's golden calf, has its own group of the sons of the prophets in Elijah's day (2 Kings 2:2–3). On the road up to Bethel after Elijah's departure, a crowd of youths from the town mocks Elisha, calling out to the bald man to go on up. He curses them in the LORD's name, and two bears from the woods maul forty-two of them (2 Kings 2:23–24). Many readers think the taunt mocked Elijah's ascension and that the town's hostility reflects Bethel's role as a royal shrine opposed to the LORD's prophets (compare Amos 7:10–13).

uncommon: The Talmud says Elisha fell ill because he cursed the youths of Bethel.

sections.h: Gilgal in the Elijah and Elisha stories (2 Kings 2; 4)
sections.b: Elijah's last journey begins at Gilgal (2 Kings 2:1), and Elisha later teaches the sons of the prophets there during a famine (2 Kings 4:38). This Gilgal may be the famous site near Jericho, but because Elijah and Elisha go down from it to Bethel, many scholars think it was a different Gilgal in the hills north of Bethel. At Gilgal a stew made with wild gourds is made safe with flour, and twenty barley loaves feed a hundred men (2 Kings 4:38–44).

uncommon: Some scholars identify this Gilgal with Jiljilia, north of Bethel, rather than the Gilgal near Jericho.

sections.h: Carmel as Elisha's base (2 Kings 2; 4)
sections.b: After the bears of Bethel, Elisha goes to Mount Carmel and then back to Samaria (2 Kings 2:25). It is at Carmel that the Shunammite finds him when her son dies; he sees her coming from far off and sends Gehazi to meet her, and she grasps his feet (2 Kings 4:25–27). The mountain of Elijah's contest with the prophets of Baal seems to have been a regular place of retreat for his successor.

uncommon: Some think Carmel held a community of prophets that Elisha visited, though the text never says so.

sections.h: The prophet's widow and her oil (2 Kings 4)
sections.b: A widow of one of the sons of the prophets cries to Elisha that a lender is coming to take her two sons as slaves for her husband's debt. Elisha asks what she has, and she has only a small flask of oil. He tells her to borrow as many empty jars as she can, shut the door, and pour; the oil flows until every jar is full and stops when there are no more. She sells it, pays the debt and lives on the rest with her sons (2 Kings 4:1–7). The story echoes Elijah and the widow of Zarephath (1 Kings 17:8–16) and the law's concern for widows and debt (Exodus 22:22–27; Leviticus 25:39–43). Later Jewish tradition and Josephus identify her as the wife of Obadiah, who hid the prophets from Jezebel.

uncommon: Josephus and the Targum say the widow's husband was Obadiah, who had borrowed money to feed the hidden prophets.

sections.h: The Shunammite's roof room (2 Kings 4; 8)
sections.b: A wealthy woman of Shunem presses Elisha to eat at her house whenever he passes, and then persuades her husband to build a small walled roof room with a bed, table, chair and lamp for the holy man of God (2 Kings 4:8–10). When Elisha offers to speak for her to the king, she answers that she lives among her own people. Her reward is the son she did not ask for (2 Kings 4:11–17). Her hospitality is remembered later when Elisha warns her of famine and the king restores her land (2 Kings 8:1–6). Readers compare her with Abraham and Sarah, whose welcome of guests was also followed by the promise of a son.

uncommon: Some readers think the Shunammite's refusal of favors shows that she wished to keep her independence from the prophet as well as the king.

sections.h: A son for the Shunammite (2 Kings 4)
sections.b: The Shunammite woman has no son, and her husband is old. Gehazi points this out, and Elisha promises that at this set time next year she will hold a son. Her reply is close to a protest: she begs him not to deceive her. The promise is kept (2 Kings 4:14–17). The wording echoes the LORD's promise to Sarah (Genesis 18:10–14). Unlike Sarah, Rachel or Hannah, the Shunammite never asks for a child, and when the boy later dies she reproaches Elisha that she did not ask for a son (2 Kings 4:28) before he is restored to her.

uncommon: The Shunammite is the only woman in the Bible promised a child she did not ask for and did not seem to want.

sections.h: Naaman, Gehazi and the four men at the gate (2 Kings 5; 7)
sections.b: Skin disease runs through 2 Kings 5–8. Naaman, Aram's great commander, has it, and the king of Israel takes his request for healing as a pretext for war, since only God kills and makes alive. Elisha tells Naaman to wash seven times in the Jordan, and his flesh becomes like a little boy's (2 Kings 5:1–14). Gehazi's greed brings Naaman's disease on him and his descendants (2 Kings 5:27). In the siege of Samaria four men with skin disease, living outside the gate as the law required, find the abandoned Aramean camp and bring the good news (2 Kings 7:3–11; Leviticus 13:46). The Hebrew tsara'at covered several conditions and is not the same as modern leprosy.

uncommon: The Talmud identifies the four men at Samaria's gate as Gehazi and his sons.

sections.h: Naaman the Aramean (2 Kings 5)
sections.b: Naaman is an enemy commander whose victories, the narrator says, the LORD had given (2 Kings 5:1). Healed in the Jordan, he declares that there is no God in all the earth except in Israel, asks for two mules' load of Israel's soil so that he can worship the LORD at home, and asks pardon in advance for bowing beside his king in Rimmon's temple. Elisha tells him to go in peace (2 Kings 5:15–19). Jesus cites Naaman to show that God's mercy reached foreigners when Israelites were passed over (Luke 4:27). Elsewhere in these chapters the Shunammite lives for seven years as a foreigner in Philistia (2 Kings 8:1–2).

uncommon: The Talmud reads Elisha's Go in peace as allowing Naaman an outward bow under compulsion, since non-Jews are not commanded to die rather than do so (Bavli Sanhedrin 74b–75a).

sections.h: No God in all the earth but in Israel (2 Kings 1; 5)
sections.b: Two confessions frame the early Elisha stories. Elijah's question to Ahaziah's messengers, whether there is no God in Israel, mocks a king who looks abroad for an oracle (2 Kings 1:3, 1:6, 1:16). Naaman, healed, says the reverse from the outside: there is no God in all the earth except in Israel (2 Kings 5:15). Yet Naaman's request for Israel's soil shows a belief that a god is tied to his land, and the wrath at Kir-hareseth in 2 Kings 3:27 has been read by some as a trace of the older idea that Chemosh had power in Moab. Readers debate how far these chapters assume that other gods exist but are powerless, and how far they deny them entirely.

uncommon: Some scholars see in Naaman's soil a stage between belief in national gods and full monotheism.

sections.h: Mesha's sacrifice of his son (2 Kings 3)
sections.b: At the height of the siege of Kir-hareseth the king of Moab takes his firstborn son, the heir to his throne, and offers him as a burnt offering on the city wall (2 Kings 3:27). The Bible forbids child sacrifice to Molech or any god and condemns Israelite kings who practiced it (Leviticus 18:21; 2 Kings 16:3; 2 Kings 21:6). Mesha's offering was probably made to Chemosh, not to Molech, but it belongs to the same practice of giving a child in extreme crisis. A Ugaritic prayer promises a firstborn to Baal when a city is attacked, and Micah later asks whether the LORD wants a firstborn for one's sins (Micah 6:7).

uncommon: A view in the Talmud held that Mesha offered his son to Israel's God, not to Chemosh.

sections.h: The campaign against Moab (2 Kings 3)
sections.b: Elisha's word to the three kings promises that the LORD will hand Moab over, and tells them to strike every fortified town, cut down every good tree, stop up every spring and ruin every good field with stones (2 Kings 3:18–19). This goes beyond the law's limits for siege warfare, which forbade cutting down fruit trees (Deuteronomy 20:19–20). The armies carry it out (2 Kings 3:24–25), but the war ends in withdrawal when great wrath comes upon Israel (2 Kings 3:27). Mesha's own inscription describes Moab's war in the same holy-war terms: he devoted the people of Nebo to destruction for his god.

uncommon: Some interpreters think the wrath of 2 Kings 3:27 was God's anger at Israel's breach of Deuteronomy 20:19.

sections.h: Great wrath upon Israel (2 Kings 3:27)
sections.b: Few verses in Kings are harder than the end of 2 Kings 3: when Mesha sacrifices his son, there comes great wrath upon Israel, and the armies go home. The Hebrew qetsef usually means God's anger, which suggests that the LORD was angry with Israel. Others read it as Chemosh's wrath, as Moab would have seen it, or as the fury of the Moabites, or as horror among the besiegers. Josephus says the kings pitied Mesha; the Greek translators wrote great regret. The text does not say whose wrath it was.

uncommon: Some critical scholars think the narrator assumed that Chemosh's anger really drove Israel out of Moab.

sections.h: The two Jehorams (2 Kings 1; 3; 8)
sections.b: 2 Kings 1–8 raises some of the hardest dating problems in Kings. Jehoram of Israel is said to begin to reign in the second year of Jehoram of Judah (2 Kings 1:17) and in the eighteenth year of Jehoshaphat (2 Kings 3:1), while Jehoram of Judah begins in the fifth year of Joram of Israel (2 Kings 8:16). Most solutions assume that Jehoram of Judah shared the throne with Jehoshaphat for some years. Ahaziah of Judah is said to begin in Joram's eleventh year (2 Kings 9:29) and his twelfth (2 Kings 8:25), a difference often explained by different ways of counting the first year. Both Joram of Israel and Ahaziah of Judah died in 841 BC, a date fixed by Assyrian records of Jehu's tribute.

uncommon: The Lucianic Greek has a different chronology for these reigns, which some scholars think is older.

sections.h: Horses and chariots of fire (2 Kings 1; 2; 6)
sections.b: The angel of the LORD speaks to Elijah twice in 2 Kings 1, once to send him to meet the king's messengers and once to tell him not to fear the third captain (2 Kings 1:3, 1:15). A chariot of fire and horses of fire separate Elijah and Elisha (2 Kings 2:11). At Dothan, Elisha prays for his frightened servant's eyes to be opened, and he sees the hill full of horses and chariots of fire around Elisha (2 Kings 6:15–17). Elisha's cry of my father, the chariots of Israel and its horsemen (2 Kings 2:12) is later said over Elisha himself (2 Kings 13:14), suggesting that the prophet was Israel's true defense.
sections.refs: 2 Kings 1:3; 2 Kings 1:15; 2 Kings 2:11–12; 2 Kings 6:15–17; 2 Kings 13:14; Psalm 34:7; Psalm 68:17

uncommon: Some scholars think the fiery chariots belong to the imagery of the LORD as a divine warrior, like Baal riding the clouds.

sections.h: Elisha and Jesus (2 Kings 2; 4; 5)
sections.b: Christian readers have long seen Elisha's wonders as a pattern for Jesus' own. Jesus raises a widow's son at Nain, near Shunem (Luke 7:11–17). He feeds crowds with a few barley loaves, with food left over (John 6:9–13; compare 2 Kings 4:42–44). He cleanses men with skin disease, and a foreigner returns to thank him (Luke 17:11–19). At Nazareth he names Naaman as a foreigner chosen for healing (Luke 4:27). Church fathers read Naaman's seven dips as a figure of baptism, and Justin Martyr saw in the floating ax head a sign of the cross. Elijah's ascension and Elisha's double share of his spirit were read as a pattern for Jesus' ascension and the gift of the Spirit in Acts.

uncommon: Some scholars think the Gospel of Luke deliberately models Jesus on Elijah and Elisha throughout.

sections.h: A lamp for David's sons (2 Kings 8)
sections.b: When Jehoram of Judah follows the ways of Ahab's house, the narrator says the LORD was not willing to destroy Judah for the sake of his servant David, as he had promised to give him a lamp for his sons for all time (2 Kings 8:19). The lamp image goes back to the promise that David would always have a descendant on the throne in Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:36; 1 Kings 15:4). Chronicles makes the covenant explicit (2 Chronicles 21:7). Even when Judah's kings marry into Ahab's house, the promise to David keeps the line alive.

sections.h: Edom with the allies and Edom in revolt (2 Kings 3; 8)
sections.b: In 2 Kings 3 a king of Edom marches with Israel and Judah against Moab, probably as Judah's vassal, since 1 Kings 22:47 says Edom then had no king but a deputy. The route goes through the wilderness of Edom, and the water comes from the direction of Edom (2 Kings 3:8–9, 3:20). Under Jehoram of Judah, Edom revolts and sets up its own king; Jehoram's night attack at Zair breaks out of an encirclement but does not restore control (2 Kings 8:20–22). The narrator notes that Edom remained free to his own day, recalling Isaac's word that Esau would one day break Jacob's yoke (Genesis 27:40).

uncommon: Some scholars think the king of Edom in 2 Kings 3 was added later, since Edom had no king at the time.

sections.h: The word of the LORD in Elisha's time (2 Kings 1–8)
sections.b: These chapters are full of prophecy spoken and fulfilled. Elijah's word that Ahaziah will die comes true (2 Kings 1:16–17). Elisha calls for a musician before the LORD's hand comes on him (2 Kings 3:15). He promises water and victory (2 Kings 3:16–20), a son (2 Kings 4:16–17), food in a famine (2 Kings 4:43–44), and flour at normal prices in a besieged city, with the officer who doubted dying as Elisha said (2 Kings 7:1–2, 7:16–20). He knows what the king of Aram says in his bedroom (2 Kings 6:12) and what Gehazi did in secret (2 Kings 5:26). In Damascus he sees Hazael's future and weeps (2 Kings 8:10–13). The repeated fulfillment formula, according to the word of the LORD, ties these stories into Kings' larger argument that God's word governs history.

uncommon: Some scholars think music was used among the prophetic guilds to bring on an ecstatic state, as in 1 Samuel 10:5.
